metadata.description: Master misconception taxonomy compiled from validated Physics Education Research instruments
sources: Force Concept Inventory (FCI) — Hestenes, Wells, Swackhamer 1992
Force and Motion Conceptual Evaluation (FMCE) — Thornton & Sokoloff 1998
Conceptual Survey of Electricity and Magnetism (CSEM) — Maloney et al. 2001
Brief Electricity and Magnetism Assessment (BEMA) — Ding et al. 2006
Determining and Interpreting Resistive Electric Circuit Concepts Test (DIRECT) — Engelhardt & Beichner 2004
Thermal Concepts Survey (TCS) — Wattanakasiwich et al. 2013
Mechanical Waves Conceptual Survey (MWCS) — Tongchai et al. 2009
Four-Tier Geometrical Optics Test (FTGOT) — Kaltakci-Gurel et al. 2017
Quantum Mechanics Conceptual Survey (QMCS) — McKagan et al. 2010
Quantum Mechanics Visualization Instrument (QMVI) — Cataloglu & Robinett 2002

misconceptions.description: Student conflates position and velocity, believing that objects at the same position must have the same velocity, or that velocity is determined by position rather than rate of change of position.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: If two objects are at the same place, they must be going the same speed.

misconceptions.description: Student conflates velocity and acceleration, believing that faster objects must have greater acceleration or that zero velocity means zero acceleration.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The car is going faster so it must be accelerating more. If it's stopped, there's no acceleration.

misconceptions.description: Student treats velocity as a scalar, ignoring its directional nature. Fails to account for direction changes as acceleration.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The car is going around the curve at a constant 30 mph so it's not accelerating.

misconceptions.description: Student interprets kinematics graphs as literal pictures of the motion path rather than as abstract representations of quantities over time.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The velocity graph goes up, so the object must be going uphill.

misconceptions.description: Student confuses the slope of a graph with its height/value. On a position-time graph, reads the position value as velocity instead of computing the slope.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The position is high on the graph, so the velocity must be high.

misconceptions.description: Student does not recognize that the area under a velocity-time graph represents displacement, or confuses area with other quantities.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: I need to read the velocity value to find how far it went, not calculate the area.

misconceptions.description: Student believes that a force applied to an object gives it an internal 'impetus' or 'force' that it carries with it and that gradually dissipates.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: When you kick a ball, you give it a force that it carries. The ball slows down because the force you gave it wears off.

misconceptions.description: Student believes that the 'impetus' or 'force' given to a moving object gradually dissipates on its own, causing the object to slow down even without external forces.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The ball eventually stops because the force you threw it with runs out.

misconceptions.description: Student believes that an object moving in a circle has a circular impetus that keeps it going in a circle, and when released, it continues briefly in a curve before going straight.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: If you whirl a ball on a string and let go, it curves outward because of the spinning motion it has.

misconceptions.description: Student believes that sustained motion requires a sustained force. If nothing is pushing it, it should stop.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The puck will stop sliding because nothing is pushing it anymore.

misconceptions.description: Student believes that only active agents (people, motors, engines) can exert forces. Passive objects like tables, walls, or floors do not exert forces.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The table doesn't push up on the book — it just holds it there. Only things that are alive or have engines push.

misconceptions.description: Student believes that if an object is moving, there must be a force on it in the direction of motion.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The ball is moving to the right, so there must be a force pushing it to the right.

misconceptions.description: Student believes that if an object is not moving, no forces act on it.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The book is sitting still on the table, so there are no forces on it.

misconceptions.description: Student believes that velocity is proportional to applied force rather than acceleration being proportional to force (Aristotelian view).
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: If I push twice as hard, the object goes twice as fast.

misconceptions.description: Student believes that for an object to accelerate, the force must be continuously increasing. Constant force means constant velocity.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: For the car to keep speeding up, you have to keep pushing the gas pedal harder and harder.

misconceptions.description: Student believes that the largest single force on an object determines its motion, rather than the net force.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: Gravity is pulling harder than the rope is pulling up, so the object goes down.

misconceptions.description: Student believes that the most recently applied force determines the motion, overriding all previous forces.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: I pushed it last, so it goes the direction I pushed, regardless of other forces.

misconceptions.description: Student believes that when multiple forces act, the object moves in a compromise direction between them rather than in the direction of the net force.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: There's a force going right and one going up, so the object goes at 45 degrees — halfway between.

misconceptions.description: Student believes that in an interaction, the more massive object exerts a greater force than the less massive one.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The truck hits the car with more force because it's heavier.

misconceptions.description: Student believes that in an interaction, the most active agent (the one 'doing' the action) produces the greatest force.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The person pushing the wall pushes harder than the wall pushes back because the person is the one doing the pushing.

misconceptions.description: Student incorrectly identifies action-reaction pairs as two forces acting on the same object rather than on two different interacting objects.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The action and reaction for a book on a table are gravity pulling it down and the table pushing it up.

misconceptions.description: Student can plug numbers into F=ma but has no conceptual understanding of what the equation means physically.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: F=ma, so force is 50N times 2kg divided by... wait, which one do I solve for?

misconceptions.description: Student applies F=ma using only one force rather than the net force, ignoring other forces acting on the object.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The applied force is 20N and mass is 5kg, so acceleration is 4 m/s^2 — I don't need to worry about friction.

misconceptions.description: Student treats energy as a material substance that is contained within objects rather than as an abstract accounting quantity.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The ball has energy inside it from being lifted up. When it falls, the energy flows out.

misconceptions.description: Student believes work depends only on distance moved, ignoring the force component and angle between force and displacement.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: I carried the box 10 meters, so I did a lot of work on it — even though I carried it horizontally.

misconceptions.description: Student believes kinetic energy depends only on mass or only on speed, not on both.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The heavier truck has more kinetic energy even though the car is going faster.

misconceptions.description: Student conflates energy and force, using the terms interchangeably or believing they are the same concept.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The ball has a lot of force because it's high up — I mean energy — aren't they the same?

misconceptions.description: Student conflates momentum with velocity, ignoring the role of mass in momentum.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The faster ball has more momentum regardless of mass.

misconceptions.description: Student conflates momentum and kinetic energy, not distinguishing that momentum is a vector proportional to v while KE is a scalar proportional to v^2.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: Momentum is conserved, so kinetic energy must be conserved too — they're basically the same thing.

misconceptions.description: Student conflates impulse with force, not understanding that impulse depends on both force and time interval.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: A bigger force always means a bigger impulse, no matter how long it acts.

misconceptions.description: Student believes that heavier objects fall faster than lighter ones in all situations, not just in the presence of air resistance.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The bowling ball falls faster than the tennis ball because it's heavier.

misconceptions.description: Student believes gravity is caused by or requires the atmosphere. No air means no gravity.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: In space there's no air so there's no gravity.

misconceptions.description: Student believes the force of gravity on an object increases as it falls, confusing increasing velocity with increasing force.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The ball speeds up as it falls, so gravity must be pulling harder the further it falls.

misconceptions.description: Student conflates angular and linear velocity, believing objects at the same angular velocity have the same linear speed regardless of radius.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: Both riders on the merry-go-round go at the same speed because they go around together.

misconceptions.description: Student believes centrifugal force is a real outward force acting on objects in circular motion, rather than a fictitious force in a rotating reference frame.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: When I spin a ball on a string, there's a force pushing it outward. If the string breaks, the ball flies outward.

misconceptions.description: Student neglects the inverse-square dependence of electrostatic force on distance, or treats it as inversely proportional to distance rather than distance squared.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: If I double the distance, the force is halved.

misconceptions.description: Student believes charging by contact means that the total charge is simply transferred rather than shared/redistributed between objects.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: When I touch the charged rod to the sphere, all the charge moves to the sphere.

misconceptions.description: Student conflates electric field with electric force, not understanding that the field exists independently of any test charge.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: If there's no charge there, there's no electric field there either.

misconceptions.description: Student interprets electric field lines as the paths that charges follow, rather than as representations of the field direction at each point.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The electron will follow the field line like a track.

misconceptions.description: Student does not understand that the electric field inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is zero, or that charges reside on the surface.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The charge is evenly distributed throughout the metal sphere.

misconceptions.description: Student fails to apply the superposition principle for electric fields, considering only the nearest or largest charge.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The field at that point is just from the closest charge — the others are too far to matter.

misconceptions.description: Student confuses the Gaussian surface (mathematical construct) with a physical surface, or believes the flux depends on the shape of the Gaussian surface rather than the enclosed charge.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: I need to use a spherical Gaussian surface because the flux would be different with a cube.

misconceptions.description: Student conflates electric flux with electric field strength, not understanding that flux is field integrated over an area.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The flux is stronger near the charge because the field is stronger there.

misconceptions.description: Student believes that current is 'used up' as it flows through a circuit — more current enters a resistor than leaves it.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The bulb uses up some of the current, so less comes out the other side.

misconceptions.description: Student believes the battery supplies a constant current regardless of the circuit it's connected to, rather than maintaining a constant voltage.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The battery pushes out the same amount of current no matter what you connect it to.

misconceptions.description: Student analyzes circuits using local reasoning — only considering the components immediately adjacent to the point of interest rather than analyzing the complete circuit.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: Adding a resistor in a different branch won't affect this bulb because it's on a different path.

misconceptions.description: Student believes current flows out of the battery and is modified sequentially by each component it encounters. Changes downstream don't affect upstream behavior.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The first bulb gets the full current, and then whatever's left goes to the second bulb.

misconceptions.description: Student conflates voltage and current, using them interchangeably or not distinguishing their roles in circuit behavior.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: More voltage means more current — they're basically the same thing.

misconceptions.description: Student adds parallel resistances directly (like series) rather than using the reciprocal formula.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: Two 10-ohm resistors in parallel give 20 ohms total.

misconceptions.description: Student does not understand that current takes the path of least resistance preferentially, or that a short circuit bypasses other components.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The current splits evenly between the wire and the resistor.

misconceptions.description: Student believes current flows through an open (broken) circuit or that a voltmeter allows current to flow through the measured component.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: There's still some current flowing even though the switch is open.

misconceptions.description: Student conflates magnetic and electric fields, applying electric field rules to magnets or vice versa.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The magnetic field pushes the charge in the direction of the field, just like an electric field.

misconceptions.description: Student incorrectly determines the direction of the magnetic force on a moving charge, failing to apply the cross-product (right-hand rule) correctly.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The force is in the direction of the magnetic field, not perpendicular to both B and v.

misconceptions.description: Student believes isolated magnetic poles (monopoles) can exist — that you can have a north pole without a south pole.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: If I break a magnet in half, one piece will be just north and the other just south.

misconceptions.description: Student believes that the presence of a magnetic field (rather than a change in magnetic flux) causes electromagnetic induction.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The coil is in a magnetic field, so there must be a current induced in it.

misconceptions.description: Student incorrectly applies Lenz's law, predicting the induced current in the wrong direction or not understanding its opposition character.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The magnetic field points down, so the induced current creates a field pointing down too.

misconceptions.description: Student conflates temperature and heat, using them interchangeably. Believes temperature measures the amount of heat in an object.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The metal has more heat because it's at a higher temperature.

misconceptions.description: Student believes that temperature depends on the size or amount of material — a larger object at the same temperature has a 'higher temperature.'
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The big pot of boiling water is hotter than the small cup of boiling water.

misconceptions.description: Student believes metals are inherently cold (or warm) because of how they feel, not understanding thermal conductivity and heat transfer rates.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The metal table feels colder than the wooden table, so the metal must be at a lower temperature.

misconceptions.description: Student believes that insulation (coats, blankets) generate heat rather than simply reducing heat transfer.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The blanket warms you up — it adds heat to your body.

misconceptions.description: Student believes that different materials in the same environment will reach different equilibrium temperatures.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The metal and wood in the same room are at different temperatures because metal feels colder.

misconceptions.description: Student treats heat or cold as a substance (caloric theory) that flows between objects, rather than understanding heat as energy transfer.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: Cold flows from the ice into your hand, making it cold.

misconceptions.description: Student believes temperature continues to rise during a phase change rather than remaining constant.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: If I keep heating ice, the temperature keeps going up even while it's melting.

misconceptions.description: Student believes that waves transport matter along with energy. The medium itself moves with the wave.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The wave carries the water forward — that's why surfers move toward shore.

misconceptions.description: Student believes that when a wave enters a new medium, its frequency changes rather than its wavelength and speed.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: When light enters glass, it changes color because the frequency changes.

misconceptions.description: Student conflates amplitude with frequency or wavelength, believing louder sounds have higher pitch or larger waves are faster.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The bigger wave has a higher frequency.

misconceptions.description: Student believes that when two waves undergo destructive interference, the energy is permanently destroyed rather than the waves passing through each other.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: When the two waves cancel out, the energy disappears.

misconceptions.description: Student believes sound travels faster (or at all) in a vacuum, not understanding that sound requires a medium.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: Sound travels fastest in space because there's nothing to slow it down.

misconceptions.description: Student believes light rays/beams are visible from the side, or that we see objects because light 'illuminates' them and our eyes passively receive the brightness.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: You can see a laser beam from the side because light is visible.

misconceptions.description: Student believes the image formed by a mirror is located on the surface of the mirror rather than behind it.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: My reflection is on the mirror surface.

misconceptions.description: Student believes covering half a lens blocks half the image rather than reducing image brightness.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: If I cover the top half of the lens, the top half of the image disappears.

misconceptions.description: Student applies subtractive (paint) color mixing rules to additive (light) color mixing or vice versa.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: Red light and green light make brown when combined, just like mixing paint.

misconceptions.description: Student interprets wave-particle duality as the object literally being both a wave and a particle simultaneously, like a wavy ball.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: An electron is a tiny ball that wobbles like a wave as it moves.

misconceptions.description: Student believes the uncertainty principle is about measurement limitations (clumsy instruments) rather than a fundamental property of nature.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: We can't measure position and momentum simultaneously because measuring one disturbs the other — with better instruments we could measure both.

misconceptions.description: Student pictures electrons as orbiting the nucleus in defined circular paths like planets, rather than existing in probability distributions.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The electron goes around the nucleus in a circle, like the Earth goes around the Sun.

misconceptions.description: Student interprets the wavefunction as a physical, material wave in space rather than a mathematical description of probability amplitude.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The wavefunction is a real wave, like a water wave, that the electron rides on.

misconceptions.description: Student believes that quantum measurement simply reveals a preexisting value rather than collapsing a superposition into a definite state.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The electron was always spin-up, we just didn't know it until we measured.

misconceptions.description: Student believes that energy levels in atoms are continuous rather than discrete/quantized.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: An electron can have any energy it wants in an atom, not just specific values.

misconceptions.description: Student thinks of a photon as a tiny classical particle (a little ball of light) rather than a quantum of the electromagnetic field.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: A photon is a tiny particle of light that bounces off things like a billiard ball.

misconceptions.description: Student visualizes quantum tunneling as the particle going over the potential barrier with enough energy rather than through it with insufficient classical energy.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The particle gets a boost of energy somehow and jumps over the barrier.

misconceptions.description: Student interprets quantum superposition as a classical statistical mixture — the system is definitely in one state, we just don't know which.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: Schrodinger's cat is either alive or dead, we just don't know which until we look.

misconceptions.description: Student believes quantization only applies at the atomic scale and has no relevance to macroscopic phenomena.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: Quantum effects only matter for atoms. Nothing quantum happens in the everyday world.

misconceptions.description: Student believes objects literally get heavier (gain mass) as they move faster, rather than understanding relativistic momentum correctly.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: As the spaceship goes faster, it gets heavier and heavier, which is why it can't reach light speed.

misconceptions.description: Student believes simultaneity is absolute — if two events are simultaneous for one observer, they are simultaneous for all observers.
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: If two lightning bolts strike at the same time, everyone agrees they happened at the same time.

misconceptions.description: Student thinks length contraction means objects actually physically compress or that you would see them as shorter (confusing measurement with visual appearance).
misconceptions.typical_student_reasoning: The spaceship physically squishes as it goes fast, like being compressed.
